docs.text: CWL and OCI in the CI runtime CWL describes a command-line tool or workflow. A workflow can refer to container images for its executable steps, but its CWL document and descriptive metadata are also useful artifacts in their own right. This runtime brings the tools for handling both into one CI environment: CWL document -> validation -> documentation and metadata -> OCI workflow artifact Container image -> scan -> registry image cwltool validates CWL. The transpiler-mate plugins derive other representations from that source, such as an OGC process description, discovery metadata, Markdown, diagrams, or an SBOM report. Generating these representations from CWL helps keep the published descriptions tied to the workflow document. ORAS publishes the CWL document and metadata together with the artifact type application/cwl . Skopeo copies container images between storage locations and registries. These operations address different objects: publishing a CWL artifact does not build or publish the executable images referenced by the workflow. Validation and scanning answer different questions CWL validation checks the document's structure and CWL rules. Conversion through cwl2ogc checks whether the selected entry point can be represented for OGC API Processes. Neither step establishes that a referenced image is free of known vulnerabilities; image scanning is a separate stage handled by Trivy. Tags and digests A tag is a convenient name for an artifact or image. A digest identifies its exact content. The build workflow captures the pushed image digest and generates notices from that image so the attachment corresponds to the published build, even if a tag later moves. Try the tutorial for a first validation, or use the publishing guide for an existing workflow.

docs.text: License reports and notices The image build produces two complementary outputs: a license scan for review and an attribution attachment for the published image. License reports Before publication, Trivy scans image.tar using supported package metadata and recognizable license text. The JSON and text reports preserve all severity levels, including UNKNOWN. Counts in the job summary help reviewers locate findings; they do not determine whether a dependency is acceptable for a particular use. The pipeline is report-only for license findings. This allows evidence to be reviewed before a blocking policy is established, while scanner or formatting errors still fail the job. Third-party notices After publication, the collector runs against the exact pushed digest. It gathers installed RPM packages, including base-image packages, Python distributions, and Helm plugin license and attribution files. Known downloaded tools are listed even when notice files are unavailable. ORAS attaches the resulting NOTICE together with the repository's LICENSE as an OCI artifact associated with the image digest. Keeping these as an attachment lets consumers retrieve attribution for that image without adding generated files to the repository or placing them inside the image. Coverage and interpretation Notice collection is best-effort. Missing notices and embedded or unmanaged dependencies remain items for review. A scan cannot establish complete dependency coverage, license compatibility, or fulfillment of source-distribution and attribution obligations. Neither a successful scan nor a generated notice is legal clearance. The retrieval guide explains where to find both outputs. The CI reference records the report settings.

docs.text: Build and run the container Use these commands from a checkout of this repository with Docker running. The Dockerfile downloads amd64 binaries, so use an amd64 environment or a Docker installation configured to emulate it. Build locally docker build -t ci-eoap-container:latest . The build needs network access to package repositories and downloaded tools. See included tools for the build inputs. Work with local files From the directory containing your CWL files, start a shell with that directory mounted at /work : docker run --rm -it \ --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp \ -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work \ ci-eoap-container:latest bash Run the commands in the other how-to guides in this shell, or in a CI job that already uses the image as its runtime. Outputs under /work persist in the host directory. Files elsewhere in this disposable container are removed on exit. For a single command, replace bash with the tool and its arguments: docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work \ ci-eoap-container:latest cwltool --validate workflow.cwl See the CI reference for published image tags.
docs.title: Build and run the container

docs.text: Maintain the documentation Run the following from the repository root with Python 3.10 or newer available. Documentation dependencies are separate from the container's Python toolchain. Preview locally python3 -m venv .venv-docs . .venv-docs/bin/activate python -m pip install -r requirements-docs.txt mkdocs serve Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 to browse the documentation. Changes under docs/ are reloaded during development. Add or edit a page Choose a location based on what the reader needs: Directory Purpose docs/tutorials/ Guided learning with a concrete example and expected results docs/how-to/ Steps to accomplish a specific task, with prerequisites docs/reference/ Factual descriptions of tools, configuration, and outputs docs/explanation/ Context, design decisions, and conceptual relationships Add the page to nav in mkdocs.yml . Use relative Markdown links between pages. Keep versions and pipeline behavior aligned with Dockerfile , requirements.txt , and .github/workflows/build-image.yaml . Configuration options are described in the MkDocs configuration reference . Build and check mkdocs build --strict The generated site is written to site/ , which is ignored by Git. The documentation workflow runs this same check on pull requests and pushes to develop and main . Strict mode rejects warnings, including broken local links and pages missing from navigation. Publishing the generated site is a separate hosting step.

docs.text: Retrieve notices and review licenses Download notices for a published image You need ORAS and pull access to the registry. Set IMAGE_REF to the exact image digest you want to inspect, replacing the placeholder before running the command: IMAGE_REF='ghcr.io/terradue/ci-eoap-container@sha256:<image-digest>' oras discover --artifact-type application/vnd.eoap.license-notices.v1 "$IMAGE_REF" Copy the attachment digest returned by discovery, then download it into a dedicated directory: mkdir -p license-notices cd license-notices oras pull 'ghcr.io/terradue/ci-eoap-container@sha256:<attachment-digest>' The attachment contains LICENSE and NOTICE . Use the attachment digest for the pull, rather than the image digest. Generate a local notice From the repository root, with the image already available to Docker: bash scripts/generate-notice.sh ci-eoap-container:latest ./NOTICE The collector runs in a disposable container. CI generates the notice after publication; a generated NOTICE does not need to be committed. Review the CI license report Open the relevant build run in GitHub Actions. Read the job summary for license entry counts by severity. Download the license-review artifact within its 30-day retention period. Inspect license-report.json and license-report.txt , including UNKNOWN entries. Findings are report-only; scanner or report-generation errors fail CI. See license reports and notices for scope and limitations and the CI reference for severity labels.
docs.title: Retrieve notices and review licenses

docs.text: Publish a CWL artifact Use ORAS in the CI runtime to publish a CWL document and its metadata to an OCI registry. You need registry push permission and the files produced by validate and transform CWL : workflow.cwl , codemeta.json , datacite.json , ogc-process.json , and ogc-record.json . Authenticate Provide REGISTRY_USER and REGISTRY_PASSWORD through your CI secret mechanism. Replace registry.example.org and the artifact repository in the commands below with your registry destination. printf '%s' "$REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | oras login registry.example.org \ --username "$REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin Push the document and metadata oras push registry.example.org/my-org/my-workflow:1.0.0 \ --artifact-type application/cwl \ ./workflow.cwl:application/cwl \ ./codemeta.json:application/json \ ./datacite.json:application/json \ ./ogc-process.json:application/json \ ./ogc-record.json:application/json ORAS prints the published artifact digest on success. Record it when downstream jobs need to identify the exact artifact. If you already have an ORAS-compatible annotations.json , add --annotation-file annotations.json to the push command. The basic example does not require an annotations file. For executable container images, use Skopeo instead. See CWL and OCI for the relationship between workflow artifacts and images.
docs.title: Publish a CWL artifact

docs.text: Scan and push container images Run these commands where Trivy and Skopeo are available, such as the CI runtime. Replace the example registry, repository, and tag with your image reference. Private registries require credentials configured for the relevant tool. Scan an image trivy image registry.example.org/my-org/my-image:1.0.0 The scanner needs access to the image and its vulnerability database. Review the report before publishing; the command above does not define a project-specific blocking policy. See the CI reference for the repository's scan settings. Push an image Authenticate to the destination registry, then copy a locally built image: printf '%s' "$REGISTRY_PASSWORD" | skopeo login registry.example.org \ --username "$REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin skopeo copy --all \ docker-daemon:my-image:1.0.0 \ docker://registry.example.org/my-org/my-image:1.0.0 The docker-daemon: source requires access to the Docker daemon that holds the image. Mounting a working directory into the runtime alone does not provide that access. When your build produces an image archive, use an archive source instead: skopeo copy \ docker-archive:image.tar \ docker://registry.example.org/my-org/my-image:1.0.0 This is the approach used by this repository's image build workflow.
docs.title: Scan and push container images

docs.text: Validate and transform CWL Run these commands inside the CI runtime from a directory containing workflow.cwl . For commands that select an entry point, set its actual CWL identifier: export WORKFLOW_ID=main Replace main with the entry point in your document. Double quotes around "workflow.cwl#${WORKFLOW_ID}" allow the shell to expand the variable. Validate CWL and OGC compatibility cwltool --validate ./workflow.cwl transpiler-mate cwl2ogc "./workflow.cwl#${WORKFLOW_ID}" --output ogc-process.json The first command validates CWL. The second checks conversion to an OGC API Processes description and writes ogc-process.json . Wrap a workflow with data staging The eoap-cwlwrap plugin and its transpiler-mate runtime are included in the container. The plugin adds stage-in and stage-out steps around the application workflow and writes a single packed CWL document. For a workflow with Directory inputs and outputs, provide compatible stage-in and stage-out CWL components in the working directory: transpiler-mate cwlwrap "./workflow.cwl#${WORKFLOW_ID}" \ --directory-stage-in ./stage-in.cwl \ --directory-stage-out ./stage-out.cwl \ --output ./wrapped.cwl cwltool --enable-ext --validate ./wrapped.cwl For File inputs or outputs, supply --file-stage-in ./stage-in-file.cwl or --file-stage-out ./stage-out-file.cwl , respectively. Supply a matching staging component for each Directory or File type present in the workflow interface; omit components for types that are absent. Staging components can also be URLs. Since version 0.32.0 , invoke transpiler-mate cwlwrap instead of the standalone eoap-cwlwrap command. Pass the source as a positional argument instead of --workflow , select the process with #${WORKFLOW_ID} instead of --workflow-id , and use --directory-stage-out instead of --stage-out . See the upstream CLI reference for all options and the wrapping guide for staging examples. Generate documentation and diagrams mkdir -p generated-docs transpiler-mate cwl2markdown ./workflow.cwl --output ./generated-docs transpiler-mate cwl2puml \ --diagrams component \ --output ./generated-docs \ --convert-image \ --image-format svg \ --puml-server uml.planttext.com \ "workflow.cwl#${WORKFLOW_ID}" transpiler-mate cwl2webgl "workflow.cwl#${WORKFLOW_ID}" \ --output "./generated-docs/${WORKFLOW_ID}-explorer.html" The SVG conversion uses the specified external PlantUML server. These commands produce workflow documentation separately from this repository's MkDocs docs/ . Generate metadata Replace the example source URL and revision with your workflow repository values: transpiler-mate cwl2codemeta \ --code-repository https://gitlab.com/example/hello.git \ --output ./codemeta.json \ workflow.cwl transpiler-mate cwl2ogcrecords ./workflow.cwl --output ogc-record.json transpiler-mate cwl2datacite workflow.cwl --output datacite.json transpiler-mate cwl2oci "workflow.cwl#${WORKFLOW_ID}" \ --image-source https://github.com/example/project \ --image-revision 4f8c2ad Generate an SBOM report transpiler-mate cwl2sbom --platform linux/amd64 --output sbom workflow.cwl This report concerns the workflow's container dependencies. The runtime image's own SBOM is generated separately by the build pipeline . To distribute the workflow and generated metadata, follow publish a CWL artifact .

docs.text: CI pipeline and artifacts The image build is defined in .github/workflows/build-image.yaml . Triggers and tags Git ref Published image tag Push to develop latest-dev Push to main latest Tag v<version> <version> , checked against release.yaml release.yaml supplies image_registry , image_prefix , image_name , and image_version . The resulting image reference is <image_registry>/<image_prefix>/<image_name>:<tag> . Build stages Resolve the image tag and validate release tags against release.yaml . Build image.tar with Kaniko without pushing. Scan HIGH and CRITICAL vulnerabilities with Trivy 0.50.2 , using --exit-code 0 . Generate an SPDX JSON SBOM with the same Trivy version. Scan licenses, format the report, and upload the review artifact. Push the archive with Skopeo and record its digest. Pull that exact digest, generate NOTICE , and attach it with LICENSE using ORAS. The image job declares contents: read and packages: write . Registry publication uses GITHUB_TOKEN ; optional Docker Hub authentication uses the dockerhub-username and dockerhub-token secrets. Outputs Output Location and purpose image.tar Build-job workspace; image archive used for scans and publication sbom.spdx.json Build-job workspace; generated runtime SBOM, no upload step is defined license-report.json , license-report.txt license-review Actions artifact, retained for 30 days pushed.digest , image.digest Build-job workspace; digest records used during publication LICENSE , NOTICE Registry attachment to the pushed image digest The notice attachment type is application/vnd.eoap.license-notices.v1 . Its files are not placed inside the runtime image. License scan settings The full license scan uses --scanners license --license-full , retains all severities, and sets --exit-code 0 . Findings do not block publication; scanner and report-generation errors fail the job. The README records these default Trivy classifications: Severity Classification CRITICAL Forbidden HIGH Restricted MEDIUM Reciprocal LOW Notice, Permissive, or Unencumbered UNKNOWN Unrecognized These are scanner labels, not a project-approved policy. See license evidence for interpretation.

Findings do not block publication; scanner and report-generation errors fail the job. The README records these default Trivy classifications: Severity Classification CRITICAL Forbidden HIGH Restricted MEDIUM Reciprocal LOW Notice, Permissive, or Unencumbered UNKNOWN Unrecognized These are scanner labels, not a project-approved policy. See license evidence for interpretation.

docs.text: Your first CWL validation In this tutorial you will build the CI image, create a small CWL document, and validate it inside the container. No registry account is needed. Before you start You need Git, a running Docker installation, an amd64 Linux container environment, and network access to download the image's dependencies. Run the commands in a Bash-compatible shell. Build the runtime Clone the repository and build the image: git clone https://github.com/Terradue/ci-eoap-container.git cd ci-eoap-container docker build -t ci-eoap-container:latest . Docker should finish by creating the local ci-eoap-container:latest image. Create a CWL document Create a separate working directory and a minimal command-line tool: mkdir -p tutorial-work cd tutorial-work cat > hello.cwl <<'EOF' cwlVersion: v1.2 class: CommandLineTool baseCommand: echo inputs: message: type: string inputBinding: position: 1 outputs: [] EOF This document describes a command that accepts a string and passes it to echo . Validate the document Mount the working directory into the container and run the validator: docker run --rm \ -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work \ ci-eoap-container:latest \ cwltool --validate hello.cwl The command should exit successfully and report that hello.cwl is valid CWL. Validation checks the document; it does not execute the described command. Generate documentation Use the same image to turn the CWL into Markdown. Pass your user and group IDs so generated files in the mounted directory belong to you: mkdir -p generated-docs docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp \ -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work \ ci-eoap-container:latest \ transpiler-mate cwl2markdown hello.cwl --output ./generated-docs ls generated-docs Open the generated Markdown to inspect the description of your tool. You have now used two tools from the same CI runtime against one mounted document. Next, use your own workflow with the transformation guide , or read why CWL and OCI are used together .
